I remember speaking to you before, you were never in the military IIRC, yes? That's one major benefit of being infantry- you learn how to really fight. You get tested so far beyond anything you thought you could accomplish, and then you exceed those expectations. And you carry these skills for life.

As an infantryman, you must stay calm. It's almost impossible to stay totally calm in combat, but you have to learn to control your panic- and the only way you can do this, is to get the body used to operating under panicked conditions. You need to simulate it. A lot of the training in the USMC for infantry involved methods that put the Marines under intense stress before/during the completion of various tasks, from marksmanship, to evacuating/treating wounded, to scaling obstacles, all the way to straight up "running for your life". Often, these tasks would be one after another, so you felt even more pressed for time and overwhelmed- overloading our systems. That's most of military training- overload your men until they adapt to that load, then pile on 2x more and repeat until you have killers ready to fight.

The US military trains us like this because the US military has a vested interest and a shit ton of money that goes into making sure we are as effective and efficient as possible. So when you're talking about stuff like preparing for bug out situations, you'll find a lot of useful information and insight from military documents and training regimens.

If you want to test yourself, start with what I suggesting in my initial comment- go to your shooting range, and run some laps around the building, do some push-ups, etc- all exercises that simulate things you might have to do while bugging out, until your heart rate is like 70% higher than resting rate. Then, try and take some shots. Compare your accuracy to your baseline. Do this over and over, and gradually you'll see that your stressed shooting looks more and more clean, closer to your relaxed optimal shooting. This also is good for the mind, as it builds confidence and determination.
